paras: The Ku-klux raid on Henry Miller was a night attack in January 1881 on the house of Miller, a Black man, near Murfreesboro in Rutherford County, Tennessee, by a band of masked men who meant to whip him for alleged arson. Miller fired on the band and escaped, and one of the raiders, a man named Newman, was killed. Most papers reported that Miller shot Newman, while the New-York Tribune said an inquest found Newman was shot by one of his own companions.

The band accused Miller of arson; the Nashville dispatch spoke of "supposed arson" and the New-York Tribune said the men wished to punish him "for burning a barn." The Murfreesboro special and the Memphis Daily Appeal called the raiders a band of "Ku-klux."

The raid took place at night, on Monday, January 3, according to the Memphis Appeal and the New-York Tribune, or on Tuesday, January 4, according to the Nashville special. In the New-York Tribune's account, four masked and armed men went to Miller's home and broke open the door after he refused to admit them. Miller opened fire, the men fired back, and he escaped by the back door.

The shorter wire versions said Miller refused to come out and killed one of the party with a shotgun, after which the band fled. The Nashville dispatch added that the mob dispersed "leaving the body where it fell." The dead man was named as L. H. Newman, L. B. Newman or Daniel Newman, and the New-York Tribune described him as being "of a good family."

According to the New-York Tribune, Miller returned the next day and found Newman's body. An inquest found that Newman had been shot by one of his own companions, and Miller was released. No report of the other raiders being identified or arrested appears in the coverage.

The story spread as a brief telegraphic item over January 6 and 7, carried from Nashville by the Chicago Daily Tribune and the Omaha Daily Bee and from New York by papers in Richmond, Savannah, Washington and Dallas. Headlines put the raider at the center: the Savannah Morning News ran "A Raider Killed," the Dallas Daily Herald "Member [of a] Mob Killed," and the Richmond Dispatch "Wouldn't Be Whipped." The Omaha Bee headed its copy "After the Wrong Negro," a phrase its text did not explain.

Within Tennessee, the Memphis Daily Appeal gave the episode one sentence in its "Tennessee Topics" column. The New-York Tribune alone printed the inquest finding, under the headline "Repelling an Attack by Masked Men," and noted the dead man's family standing. None of the reports commented on the raid beyond these facts.

The reports differ on who killed Newman: the Nashville and New York wires and the Memphis Appeal said Miller shot him, while the New-York Tribune said the inquest proved a companion fired the fatal shot. The Tribune's version is the only one that rests on an inquest finding.

reader.title: Ku-klux raid on Henry Miller
bases: A masked night band, called 'Ku-klux' in the Tennessee dispatches, went to a Black man's house to whip him for alleged arson; the only death was one of the band [A1, A3, A4].

A band of masked men came to whip Henry Miller for alleged arson, but Miller was not killed or hurt; the man who died, Newman, was a member of the band, shot either by Miller or, according to an inquest, by a companion [A1, A4, A5].
A Nashville special [A1, A2], the Memphis Appeal [A3], a New York wire [A5] and the New-York Tribune [A4] agree on the raid and Newman's death, though they differ on who fired the fatal shot.

accounts.gist: A Ku-klux or masked band came to whip Miller for arson; he refused to come out and shot one of them, Newman, dead, and the band fled leaving the body.

accounts.label: Memphis Appeal state roundup
accounts.gist: On Monday night a band of kuklux called on Miller in Rutherford County to open the door, and he shot and killed L. B. Newman.

accounts.label: New-York Tribune (inquest)
accounts.gist: Four masked, armed men broke open Miller's door on Monday night; shots were exchanged and Miller escaped; an inquest found Daniel Newman was shot by one of his companions, and Miller was released.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Murfreesboro special in a few lines under headlines centered on the band, such as 'A Raider Killed', 'Member of a Mob Killed' and 'Wouldn't Be Whipped'.
The Omaha Bee headed the Nashville special 'After the Wrong Negro' without explaining the phrase in its text.
The New-York Tribune headed its fuller version 'Repelling an Attack by Masked Men' and added that Newman 'was of a good family'.
